articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo exclusively releases new song on CD at an OC record store
articles.description: https://instagram.com/p/DcUJVk0AQiV • Next week, Olivia Rodrigo launches her Daisy Chain Fields festival in Irvine, CA., and in addition to spending the lead up to the event discussing the charities involved, she's been recruiting local businesses for the event. And now she's teamed up with a local independent record store to release a new song. • The song, 'serena joy' comes from the You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love sessions, but was cut from the main album. Olivia provided 500 CDs to the record shop, and it quickly sold out. The social media post seems to indicate that the song will be more widely available on Monday as preparations for the festival are in full swing. • The song title takes inspiration from the character of Serena Joy from The Handmaid's Tale (1985). The main character, Offred, notes that pre-Gilead, Serena Joy had been a singer and then an advocate for the continued subjection of women. Serena Joy's side wins but Offred offers a window to what victory looks like for her: "She doesn’t make speeches anymore...She stays in her home, but it doesn’t seem to agree with her. articles.description: The presenter and journalist used the Psychedelic Furs to soothe teenage heartbreak and had a Damascene moment to Bowie, but which cheesy 70s ballad does he secretly adore? The first song I fell in love with I loved a fellow sixth-former, Sarah, at school. It was unrequited. She kissed me once at the end-of-term party. I came home at 5am and played Love My Way by the Psychedelic Furs 18 times in my bedroom as the sun came up and my adult life began. The song that is my karaoke go-to I once cleared a bar in the US by singing Losing My Religion by REM. I’m looking for another chance to let rip on it, although Stan by Eminem might be better. articles.title: CARTOON: The time bomb
“Which Renaissance Workshop Would You Apprentice In?”: 25 Questions To Find Out
articles.description: Every era needs its specialists, and the Renaissance had a particularly stubborn approach to figuring out where you belonged. You didn't pick a trade; you got handed to a master, learned by watching, and eventually became someone who could spot a stone set wrong from across a room. This quiz asks the small tells that separate a cartographer from a goldsmith from someone born to run a print shop. Answer as yourself, not as who you'd like to be assigned to.
